strengths: Addresses important and underexplored problem of one-to-many Socratic teaching in medical education
Comprehensive system design with thoughtful components (personality-script decoupling, multi-dimensional thinking, three-axis reward rubric)
Extensive experimental evaluation using multiple methodologies (automated evaluation, expert assessment, user study)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component
Scalability and robustness analysis showing stable performance across varying student numbers and types
Well-documented methodology with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
20% improvement over base model with low variance suggesting reliable performance
Practical relevance addressing clinical educator scarcity
weaknesses: Circular evaluation problem: model trained on ClinEdu simulator data and then evaluated primarily through redeployment into same simulator, raising generalization concerns
Severely limited real-world validation with only 3 medical undergraduates in user study; insufficient to claim practical utility
No learning outcome measurement; cannot establish whether model actually improves student learning or only optimizes for evaluation metrics
LLM-based simulated students may not reflect real learner behavior including unpredictability, resistance patterns, and genuine confusion
Reward design and LLM judge scoring lack external validation; inter-rater reliability among LLM judges not reported
Training data primarily from single source (MedXpertQA); generalization to diverse clinical scenarios unclear
Missing statistical significance testing; standard deviations reported but no hypothesis tests
Incomplete error analysis with only one case study; no systematic assessment of failure modes or when multi-student management degrades
Baseline comparisons complicated by significant parameter differences (7B vs 70B+ models); performance gap with larger models less impressive than claimed 20% improvement
Overstated claims in abstract ('surpassing o3' when scores are 8.64 vs 8.52, within noise)

strengths: Addresses important problem in medical education (training accessibility) with well-motivated multi-agent system design
Novel application of one-to-many Socratic teaching via LLMs; clever decoupling of patient script from persona enables scenario diversity
Multi-faceted evaluation combining automated assessment, human expert review (n=3), and real user study demonstrates commitment beyond benchmarks
Thoughtful pedagogical design with multi-dimensional thinking framework captures complexity of group teaching (history, question, individual students, group dynamics)
Comprehensive system implementation with clear separation of concerns among agents (Patient, Students, Specialist, Safety Supervisor, Teacher)
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Claims of 'surpassing o3' are contradicted by data—Table 2 shows o3 (8.42) > MedTutor-R1 (8.35) on MedXpertQA; Table 4 shows marginal ~1.5% improvement. Abstract misrepresents results.
CRITICAL: Code repository is blank despite abstract claiming 'Code is released'; Dataset not released. Reproducibility is severely compromised—others cannot replicate without models, data, and code.

No actual learning outcome measurement—only proxy pedagogical metrics (ETS, MSM, MPS). Does MedTutor-R1 help students learn medicine better? Real user study with only 3 undergraduates cannot answer this.

Evaluation architecture is circular: LLMs generate data → SFT training → RL optimization using LLM judges → automated evaluation with LLM-as-judge. No sensitivity analysis on judge model choice; potential for systematic bias.

Dataset quality not validated: 300 personas generated by LLMs with no verification of realism, diversity, or clinical plausibility. Socratic decompositions lack inter-rater agreement statistics or quality criteria details.
Weak experimental baselines: 20% improvement over 7B base model (Qwen2.5VL) is modest; no comparison to stronger models or existing educational systems. Missing comparison to human tutors.
Ablation study suggests RL itself drives performance (7.69→8.35), not the specific 3-axis rubric; individual reward components show minimal individual effects, questioning rubric design contribution.
Small standard deviations across diverse models (0.09–0.35) appear suspicious; only 3 independent runs; no significance testing or multiple comparison corrections performed.
All training and most evaluation use simulated students—no validation with real learners having diverse backgrounds, prior knowledge, misconceptions, or learning styles.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an important gap in medical education (one-to-many Socratic instruction)
Sophisticated multi-agent simulation architecture with innovative decoupling of patient scripts and personas
Substantial dataset contribution (ClinTeach: 48K dialogues across 17 specialties) with systematic construction via question decomposition
Comprehensive evaluation combining automated interaction-based assessment, human expert review (κ=0.79), and real user study
Technical soundness of the SFT + RL framework with thoughtful three-axis reward rubric incorporating safety mechanisms
Strong interpretability through multi-dimensional thinking tags enabling reflection on dialogue history, objectives, individual students, and group dynamics
Clear presentation with detailed methodology sections and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Demonstrated robustness across varying numbers of students (1-10) with stable performance where baselines degrade
weaknesses: Overstated claims about 'surpassing o3': human expert evaluation shows only 0.12-point difference (8.64 vs 8.52), within measurement noise and potentially not statistically significant
Extremely limited real user study (n=3 medical undergraduates) insufficient for drawing conclusions about practical utility and generalizability

No validation on actual student learning outcomes—evaluation relies entirely on simulation-based pedagogical metrics without evidence of improved exam performance, retention, or clinical reasoning in real settings
Reward model validation concerns: GPT-4.1 judge reliability not validated against actual learning outcomes; κ=0.79 is moderate, not strong; harsh veto mechanism (-15.0 penalty) adequacy unexplored
Heavy reliance on LLMs for dataset construction (300 personas, question decomposition) with limited validation that synthetic data reflects realistic medical education dynamics and diversity
Lack of statistical significance testing throughout; standard deviations reported but no t-tests, confidence intervals, or ANOVA to verify claimed improvements are significant
Scalability analysis shows concerning baseline degradation (Med-SocraticLM drops ~15% with 10 students) but lacks investigation into causes—potential evaluation confounds
Incremental novelty: core components (SFT+RL, multi-agent simulation, Socratic method) are established; extension of prior work (SocraticLM, MEDCO) is relatively straightforward
Missing critical ablations: no analysis of multi-dimensional thinking contribution, reward axis weights, or when/why guide-review-revise rejects guidance
Limited bias analysis for simulated personas and datasets; no ethical discussion of deployment contexts, failure modes, or when to use vs. replace human instruction

strengths: Well-motivated one-to-many alignment problem with clear motivation (performance cliff in Figure 1c)
Comprehensive end-to-end framework from simulation to deployment with thoughtful design (decoupled scripts/personas, guide-review-revise workflow)
Rigorous multi-method evaluation including 200-person user study, robustness analysis across 6+ model types, scalability testing (1-10 students), and error injection experiments
Safety-first design with dual Specialist/Safety agents, multi-axis reward with hard constraints, and detailed reward-hacking mitigation analysis
Strong empirical results: 20% improvement over base model, parity with GPT-4o, particularly strong MSM scores (8.55 vs 8.39) demonstrating group management effectiveness
Excellent reproducibility with detailed prompt engineering (Figures 7-27), algorithmic specification, and commitment to release code/data
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (simulator fidelity, text+image only, short-term study, vision-language scope) and transparent discussion of tradeoffs
weaknesses: Critical simulation-reality gap: dataset entirely from LLM-generated simulators; all 300 student personas and patient personas synthetic with no evidence of robustness to real student behaviors deviating from archetypes
Misleading 'vision-language agent' framing—actually constrained to text + static images, excluding critical clinical modalities (ECG, vital signs, physical exam, auscultation, procedure video)
Learning outcomes not measured: user study only assesses satisfaction (IQ/IE/OR ratings); lacks pre/post knowledge assessments, retention studies, or clinical reasoning gains

Theory of Mind implementation overstated: mechanism is XML-tagged structured prompting (simple engineering) without evidence of genuine ToM modeling in cognitive science sense; unclear advantage over 'just prompt for individual + group analysis'
Limited expert evaluation (100/500 cases, 3 experts, κ=0.79); automated metrics rely on LLM judges; no longitudinal outcome data
Weak baseline independence: DRLTutor trained on same ClinTeach dataset; no comparison to simpler alternatives like fine-tuned GPT-4 with explicit group-state prompting

Scalability claims under-supported: 'sub-5s latency for 10 students' cited but actual numbers not provided; explicit per-student reasoning chains suggest O(N) growth; real classroom sizes (20-30) untested

Reward function design concerns: serious hacking behaviors identified in Appendix D; veto rate drop from 8-12% to <2% suggests shifted rather than solved issues; limited confidence in final robustness
Generalization unvalidated: evaluation confined to medical education; claims about general one-to-many alignment problem not empirically supported; no cross-specialty or cross-domain testing
Missing critical analyses: no failure case studies, latency breakdowns, computational costs, adversarial evaluation, or student-agent mismatch analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in clinical education AI; clear one-to-many alignment challenge is underexplored
Thoughtful system architecture with decoupled objectives/personas and guide-review-revise workflow demonstrating careful design
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation combining simulation, expert assessment (3 evaluators), and real user study (n=200)
Explicit internal reasoning mechanism with separate student belief state tracking improves interpretability vs. black-box alternatives
Extensive documentation with detailed rubrics and prompts supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates robustness across diverse student agent types and error correction in controlled experiments
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core methods (fine-tuning, GRPO, chain-of-thought) are well-established; contribution is primarily engineering rather than algorithmic advancement
Critical validity gap: entire empirical foundation relies on ClinEdu simulation; no actual learning outcome measurements despite claims to 'democratize clinical education'

Overstated superiority claims: Table 2 shows ClinTutor-R1 (8.35) underperforms o3 (8.42) and GPT-4o (8.47) on primary benchmark; human expert evaluation claims (surpass o3) based on only 100 samples with 3 evaluators

Evaluation rigor issues: primary evaluation uses LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with potential proprietary model bias; no significance testing; real user study lacks control group, pre-post learning measures, and has selection bias (voluntary medical students)
Weak ablation results: removing RL drops performance only 7.8% (8.35→7.58); removing thinking mechanism only 5% (8.35→7.79), suggesting components may be over-engineered
Reward hacking mitigation unconvincing: veto mechanism transition from 8-12% to <2% appears too clean; limited evidence of actual harmful behaviors observed vs. simply constrained

Simulation-to-reality gap not adequately addressed: text-based simulation cannot capture real ward dynamics, time pressure, patient complexity; 200-participant study uses only subjective ratings with no learning outcome validation
Reproducibility concerns: GitHub link is placeholder; code contingent on acceptance; missing details on data sourcing and implementation choices
Limited baseline comparisons: medical education agent baselines appear weaker than expected; no comparison with actual human instructor performance on same rubric
Vision-language scope misalignment: paper claims 'vision-language agent' but limited to text and static images, no audio/video/dynamic ward data despite framing

strengths: Novel problem formulation: One-to-many alignment in education is underexplored and well-motivated; clearly articulates challenges (context dilution, goal misalignment) distinct from dyadic instruction

Thoughtful system design: Decoupled patient script/persona enables scalability; Guide-Review-Revise workflow with independent Specialist/Safety agents is a sensible approach to preventing factual errors and safety violations

Comprehensive evaluation: Combines automated metrics, 3-expert evaluation (κ=0.79), and 200-participant real user study; includes robustness analysis (heterogeneous students), error correction analysis, and scalability testing (1-10 students)

Strong empirical results: 20% improvement over base model, competitive with GPT-4o, robust scalability (maintains 8.2 score with 10 students while baselines drop to ~6.6), 88.5% error correction success rate

Multi-agent simulator (ClinEdu) as reusable resource: Decoupling objective medical scripts from subjective personas with 300 patient personas and 300 student personas enables generating diverse scenarios; could benefit future research

Transparency and reproducibility: Clearly acknowledges limitations (simulator-reality gap, text+static images only, no longitudinal learning measures); detailed documentation and promised code/data release; explicit discussion of reward-hacking mitigation
Practical significance: Addresses real need in medical education; could democratize access to high-quality clinical instruction in resource-limited settings
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (SFT, GRPO, rubric-based RL) are standard; novelty lies primarily in problem formulation and system engineering rather than algorithmic innovation, which is a constraint for top-tier ML venues

Critical gap in educational evaluation: User study measures satisfaction (IQ, IE, OR) but does NOT measure actual learning outcomes, clinical reasoning improvement, or knowledge gains; no pre/post assessments; longitudinal studies absent—this is disqualifying for an educational system

Simulator-to-reality gap underexplored: Student behavior entirely from LLM personas (300 of them), not real students; real students exhibit complexity (emotion, motivation drift, procrastination) not captured; only brief claim about 'noisier real human learners' without evidence of transfer

Dataset limitations: Only 17/48k dialogues are multi-turn (max 3 turns, 3 students); derived via question decomposition + simulation, not real ward rounds; unclear if learned patterns transfer to actual clinical settings; no diversity/coverage analysis

Vision-language scope severely limited: Restricted to text + static images (no audio auscultation, physical exam signals, video)—fundamentally misaligned with title 'vision-language agent' and undermines real clinical applicability despite being positioned as a full solution

Computational efficiency underspecified: Claims 'sub-5s latency' but acknowledges 'approximately linear latency growth with number of students'; actual latency profile for 10-student cohort with per-student explicit thinking unclear; practical deployment feasibility questionable

Weak baseline comparisons: GPT-4o and o3 are general-purpose models, not medical tutors; SocraticLM (specialized baseline) is weakest comparison; no comparison to other multi-agent educational systems or domain-specific medical tutoring frameworks

Incomplete ablation studies: Table 2 shows w/o thinking: 7.94 vs 8.35 (0.41 point improvement), but mechanism of thinking's contribution not deeply analyzed; no ablation on reward rubric weights or structure; reward veto mechanism is crude (hard binary threshold)

Generalization unproven: Approach is highly specific to clinical domain; three-axis rubric is domain-dependent; unclear if method scales to other educational contexts or other one-to-many scenarios beyond pedagogy
